posts.title: From seashells to stablecoins: a very short history of how we pay for things
posts.author: Jorge Fernandez
posts.snippet:
From seashells to stablecoins: a very short history of how we pay for things

Humans have always needed a way to say "I owe you" or "we're even." That story keeps evolving, and it's moving faster than most of us can track.

It started with barter. You had chickens, I had grain, we traded. Simple, but limited: it only worked if we both happened to want what the other had.

Then came fiat currency: coins and paper backed by a government's promise rather than a physical good. Suddenly value could move across distance and time.

Checks came next, a promise on paper that a bank would honor. Then plastic: debit and credit cards, letting us pay without carrying cash at all.

Today we've gone fully digital, and this is where things get confusing fast.

Two things people often lump together that are actually opposites

You'll hear "CBDC" and "crypto" tossed around like they're the same category. They're not, and the difference matters.

A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is a digital version of a country's official currency, issued and controlled directly by that country's central bank. Every transaction can be tracked, and the issuing authority can see, and potentially restrict, how you use your own money. 

That's where my opinion comes in: a system where a central authority can watch every payment you make feels less like innovation and more like something out of Orwell's 1984. That should give pause to anyone that values their liberty and their privacy.

Bitcoin and stablecoins are a different animal entirely

Bitcoin is digital, but nobody controls it. No bank, no government, no company. It runs on a decentralized network of computers worldwide, verified by cryptography rather than a central authority. That's the whole point: value you can hold and move without asking anyone's permission.

Stablecoins are digital dollars (or euros, or other currencies), issued by private companies and designed to hold a steady value, usually backed by real reserves like cash or short-term government debt. They give you the speed of crypto with the price stability of a currency you already trust, and you don't need a bank to intermediate the transaction and can send money to another country over a weekend. 

So, here's the real distinction: CBDCs centralize control. Bitcoin and stablecoins, whatever their differences from each other, decentralize it. One tracks you by design. The others were built specifically so no one has to.

Here's the part that actually matters for you

None of this replaced anything that came before. Cash still works. Checks still clear. Your debit or credit card still swipes, or taps. You can still trade your neighbor eggs for tomatoes or legal/medical/accounting services if you want to.

What's changed is that you now have more ways to pay than any generation in history, and for the first time, some of those choices don't require anyone's permission or oversight to use.
 
That's not a small thing. That's the consumer winning.
posts.reason: Jorge's CBDC vs. crypto distinction is conceptually sound but reads as libertarian commentary rather than inviting technical legal discussion that Lemur's target audience needs.

posts.title: "Which licence should we get?" is the wrong question — and it costs founders a lot of money. The right one: "which regulatory home matches where my money actually flows?"
posts.author: Ksenia Babochkina
posts.snippet:
"Which licence should we get?" is the wrong question — and it costs founders a lot of money. The right one: "which regulatory home matches where my money actually flows?"
 
Same product can live under five different frameworks. Here's the practitioner's map — from taking real projects through each of them at Medici Expert:
 
🇨🇦 Canada MSB (FINTRAC) — technically a registration, not a licence, and that's exactly its power: one perimeter covering fiat + crypto (exchange, transfers, PSP activity), no capital requirements, no local-office theatre, months not years. The fast global anchor while you prove traction. What it's not: an EU passport or an institutional brand.
 
🇪🇺 MiCA CASP — the passport play: one authorisation → 27 EU markets, retail included. The price: real substance, capital requirements, governance, and a regulator who actually reads your whitepaper. Worth it when the EU is your market — overkill when it's "maybe later."
 
🇦🇪 VARA (Dubai) — the institutional signal. Activity-based permissions (custody, exchange, transfer, lending — each its own leg), paid-up capital per activity, 9–12 months of genuine dialogue with the regulator. Expensive, demanding — and nothing opens doors with banks, funds and Gulf partners like it. The licence you get when you're building a moat, not testing a hypothesis.
 
🇭🇰 Hong Kong MSO — the Asia corridor key: remittance and FX under one licence, credibility for APAC flows. Requires an MLRO who personally shows up to regulator interviews. Hong Kong checks.
 
🇨🇭 Swiss SRO — the quiet aristocrat. Not a licence — a self-regulatory membership under FINMA's supervision framework, covering exchange and custody below the banking threshold. And "Swiss-regulated" still does things to an investor's face no offshore stamp can.
 
The honest pattern after dozens of these projects:
 → Testing a hypothesis? Canada — or sometimes no licence at all: clean structure + a defensible legal opinion
 → EU retail is the business? MiCA
 → Institutional money, Gulf, longevity? VARA
 → Asian payment corridors? MSO
 → Conservative LPs and wealth? SRO
 
Two things stay true across all five:
 
The licence isn't the strategy. It's the shadow your money flow casts on a map.
These rulebooks move — MiCA guidance keeps landing, VARA updates its rulebooks, FINTRAC tightens reporting. A licence is a living obligation, not a trophy on the shelf.
 
We've walked clients through every framework on this list — the fast ones, the heavy ones, and the "actually, you don't need a licence yet" ones, which is sometimes the most valuable answer of all.
 
If you're mapping your own product against this list and the answer isn't obvious — that's normal. It's rarely obvious. Happy to compare notes — DMs open 👇
 
And to my fellow compliance people: what did I miss? There's always a sixth option in the comments 🙂
 
#Crypto #Licensing #MiCA #VARA #Compliance #SRO
posts.reason: Ksenia's post is a detailed practitioner's guide to choosing the right crypto regulatory framework across jurisdictions—exactly the decision-making conversation Lemur's target founders and GCs are having.

On the 'testing a hypothesis, no licence at all' branch - where do you draw the line on when a defensible legal opinion on token classification stops being enough and triggers an actual registration requirement, especially once secondary trading starts?

This matches what we see in CASP authorisation work in Slovenia - founders arrive wanting to know 'which licence' and leave the first call with a much narrower question about where their fiat rails and their token flows actually sit.

Muhammad Junaid|Jul 09, 2026|Updated 14 hours ago : ,Pakistan Observer REPOSTED ON 22-09-2026
ISLAMABAD – For years, Muslims debated whether cryptocurrency is in line with Islamic laws or its the other case. Now, one of the most influential voices in Islamic finance Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani weighed in, declaring cryptocurrency trading and investment impermissible under Shariah.
Usmani issued new fatwa declaring cryptocurrency trading and investment haram under Islamic law, a ruling that is likely to have a significant impact on Muslim investors in Pakistan and beyond.
The fatwa issued under the supervision of Darul Uloom Karachi and circulated by scholars affiliated with the institution, states that cryptocurrencies, blockchain-based crypto tokens, and stablecoins, including USDT, do not qualify as “wealth” or “property” according to the principles of Islamic jurisprudence. Because they do not meet this fundamental Shariah requirement, the ruling concludes that buying, selling, trading, or investing in these digital assets is not permissible.
 The ruling applies not only to well-known cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, but also to blockchain-issued crypto tokens and stablecoins. It further emphasizes that changing the terminology of an asset does not change its religious status. Whether described as a cryptocurrency, virtual currency, token, or stablecoin, all such digital assets are treated the same under the fatwa.
According to the ruling, the issue is not the technology behind blockchain itself but the Shariah status of the digital assets created on it. The fatwa argues that these assets fail to satisfy the Islamic legal definition of wealth, making commercial transactions involving them impermissible.
The opinion has also been endorsed by several Islamic scholars, reinforcing its standing within Pakistan’s religious community. Although a fatwa is not legally binding, Mufti Taqi Usmani is regarded as one of the world’s most influential authorities on Islamic finance. As a result, his views are expected to carry considerable weight among Muslims evaluating whether to invest in cryptocurrencies.
The ruling comes amid continued global debate over the compatibility of cryptocurrencies with Islamic law. Islamic scholars remain divided on the issue. Those who oppose cryptocurrencies argue that they involve excessive uncertainty (gharar), speculative trading, and characteristics that prevent them from being recognized as legitimate wealth under Shariah principles.
Others, however, contend that some digital assets may be permissible if they serve genuine economic purposes, achieve widespread acceptance, and are used responsibly rather than for gambling or high-risk speculation. Even scholars who take this more permissive view continue to prohibit practices involving interest (riba), fraud, excessive leverage, deception, and market manipulation.

posts.title: Have you ever heard of copyright and wondered what it actually means?
posts.author: Ebubechukwu David
posts.snippet:
Have you ever heard of copyright and wondered what it actually means?

Then read through to get enlightened.

Copyright is a branch of Intellectual Property law that protects original literary, artistic, musical, audiovisual and other creative works.

The owner of copyright enjoys exclusive rights over the protected work, including both economic and moral rights, subject to the limitations provided by law.

However, an important distinction must be made:

Copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself.

In other words, the law protects how an idea is expressed, rather than the idea in its abstract form.

To every creative: Do not wait until your work is copied before you start thinking about protecting it. Your creativity has value, and anything that has value deserves protection.

Create. Protect. Own your work.

posts.title: Tenth and final in the series.
posts.author: Jean-Paul Rudd
posts.snippet:
Tenth and final in the series.

A US court recently had to decide whether a broadly worded exclusion for "conversion, misappropriation, commingling, improper use, theft, embezzlement or defalcation of funds, account information or other property" was wide enough to catch a copyright infringement claim brought against a real estate agency. The insurer argued that using an architect's drawings without permission amounted to "misappropriation" or "improper use" of "other property." The court disagreed. It read the exclusion in context - the specific words around it all pointed to financial wrongdoing, not intellectual property disputes. Reading "other property" broadly enough to cover copyright would have stripped the specifically listed terms of any independent meaning and would have cut out exactly the kind of professional risk an errors and omissions policy for a real estate agency is supposed to cover.

The lesson for insurers: if you want an exclusion to reach copyright or other intangible rights, say so. A court will not read it in from a general residual phrase tacked onto a list of financial wrongs.

That wraps up the series - thank you to everyone who followed along.

posts.title: "Why did Flipkart—built in India for Indian shoppers—set up its parent holding company in Singapore?" 🛑
posts.author: Tanuj Khandelwal
posts.snippet:
"Why did Flipkart—built in India for Indian shoppers—set up its parent holding company in Singapore?" 🛑

If you audit the cap tables of India’s biggest tech giants, you’ll notice an identical pattern: Flipkart, Razorpay, Groww, and PhonePe all externalized their holding structures offshore.

It wasn't an accident. It was a calculated legal and tax survival strategy known as the "Flip".

Here is the exact corporate breakdown founders and investors need to know:

🔍 1. The FDI Policy Survival Play (2011–2012) A decade ago, India’s Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) laws strictly prohibited 100% foreign funding in inventory-based B2C e-commerce. To absorb billions in global venture capital without regulatory paralysis, Flipkart split into two tiers: • Flipkart Pvt. Ltd. (Singapore): Held the parent cap table, owned global IP, and absorbed international institutional capital. • Flipkart Internet Pvt. Ltd. (India): Operated strictly as a compliant B2B marketplace and technology service provider under permissible FDI norms.

🔍 2. Zero Capital Gains & Tax Efficiency Global venture funds (Tiger Global, SoftBank, Accel) often mandated offshore jurisdictions: • Singapore levies 0% tax on capital gains and 0% tax on dividend distribution. • Exits and secondaries bypassed cumbersome withholding tax frictions and complex domestic regulatory gates.

🔍 3. Flexible Corporate Governance & ESOP Pools Singapore corporate law offered: • Seamless issuance of dual-class shares and Differential Voting Rights (DVRs). • Neutral dispute resolution through the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC). • Unrestricted global ESOP pools without strict RBI/FEMA friction.

⚠️ The Big Plot Twist: "The Great Reverse Flip"
Offshore holding structures solved early-stage global fundraising. But today, the corporate architecture is reversing.

Why have giants like PhonePe, Groww, and Flipkart executed massive cross-border restructurings to shift their domiciles back to India?

The Indian Public Market Boom: Domestic retail and institutional investors now award tech firms premium public market valuations. Listing on the NSE/BSE as an Indian-domiciled entity is far cleaner than navigating cross-border listing friction.

Regulatory & Tax Normalization: With liberalized overseas investment (ODI/FDI) rules and GIFT City frameworks, running duplicate holding entities abroad now creates unnecessary corporate overhead.

💡 The Strategic Takeaway for Founders: Your corporate entity is not a static setup—it is an evolving capital architecture. Where you incorporate at Seed stage must align with your Series B fundraising, IP protection, and ultimate domestic IPO exit.

posts.title: Two federal litigators in New York submitted a formal legal brief in federal court citing six judicial decisions with official case law citations:
posts.author: Jonathan Baraldi
posts.snippet:
Two federal litigators in New York submitted a formal legal brief in federal court citing six judicial decisions with official case law citations:
* Varghese v. China Southern Airlines
* Martinez v. Delta Air Lines
* Shaboon v. EgyptAir

There was just one problem:
Not a single one of those cases existed.
ChatGPT had invented every citation, docket number, and judicial quote out of thin air.

When the judge demanded copies of the opinions, the attorneys asked ChatGPT if the cases were real.
The AI assured them with 100% confidence: "Yes, these cases are genuine and can be found in federal law reporters."

The judge issued sanctions. The attorneys' careers suffered irreparable public damage.

Why did this happen?
Because LLMs do not have an internal database of truth—they have an association engine. In legal and regulatory domains, the model's training loss rewards fluent legalese over factual existence.

When an LLM hallucinates legal or compliance citations, it doesn't sound hesitant. It cites docket formats, quotes non-existent judges, and mimics federal appellate syntax with absolute perfection.

External text filters and LLM-as-a-judge wrappers cannot catch this because the syntax passes every standard coherence check.

When TrueLLM detects that the model is synthesizing novel citations without grounded weight recall, it trips the circuit breaker in <1.5s before the legal tokens are streamed to the user.

In high-stakes enterprise compliance, fluent fiction is the most expensive failure mode in tech.

Litigation. Law firms. In-house. Compliance. Policy. Legal tech. Dispute resolution. Legal operations. Research. Academia.

None of these should feel like last-minute discoveries.

By the time students reach placement season, they are already being asked to make choices about internships, PPOs, specialisation and careers.

But how do you choose well if you have barely seen what the choices look like?

Your career exposure needs to begin much earlier.
Not with one placement talk in the final year.

With real conversations in Years 1 and 2.
What does a day in this role actually look like?
What skills matter?
What does starting pay realistically look like?
What kind of personality enjoys this work?
What internships help you test whether it is for you?

Students should have enough exposure to say:
“I can see myself doing this.”
And equally:
“This is definitely not for me.”
Both are useful discoveries.

I would much rather see a student change direction in Year 2 than realise in Year 5 that they were choosing from careers they never properly understood.

Lessons From Traditional Transit..

The Original "Auto-Pilot": Meme / Video Teaches Us About Modern Tech and Sustainable Logistics 🚀

We’ve all seen the viral video of the "Desi Tesla"—a farmer fast asleep on a wooden bullock cart while his pair of oxen confidently guides the vehicle down a paved highway. It usually gets a good laugh, but if you look past the humor, there is a fascinating masterclass in resilient infrastructure, regional adaptation, and zero-emission logistics.

Long before modern algorithms, human civilizations relied on Traditional Animal Intelligence (AI). These animals learn fixed daily routes, read environmental cues, and navigate hazards independently. 

As the iconic agricultural visionary Dr. M.S. Swaminathan once accurately noted: “Draught animals are the silent engines of our rural economy, providing energy security where machines cannot reach."

This isn't just a relic of the past. Today, Draught Animal Power (DAP) remains a massive economic driver globally:

🌱 Smallholder Resilience: For the 80%+ of global farmers managing small or marginal land holdings, high-tech tractors are financially out of reach. Animal-drawn vehicles (ADVs) provide an affordable lifeline.

🛠️ Frugal Innovation: Across agrarian hubs, communities are retrofitting traditional carts with scrap automotive ball bearings and pneumatic rubber tires. This minor engineering shift slashes physical animal strain by half while doubling payload capacities.

🌍 Hyper-Local Sustainability: From hauling sugarcane to moving organic manure, these systems represent a fully operational, zero-emission supply chain.

Different environments have spawned their own hyper-optimized "autonomous fleets":

1. Water Buffaloes: The elite marsh navigators of Southeast Asia, thriving in water-logged rice paddies.

2. Camels: Operating the ultimate desert logistics network over deep, shifting sands.

3. Mules & Yaks: The high-altitude terrain specialists that heavy machinery simply cannot match.

Innovation isn’t always about building a more complex machine or writing more code. Sometimes, it’s about recognizing, respecting, and optimizing the zero-emission systems that have reliably powered our world for thousands of years.

As the legendary polymath ‘Leonardo da Vinci’ beautifully put it:
"Nature is the source of all true knowledge. She has her own logic, her own laws, she has no effect without cause nor invention without necessity."

Let’s keep innovating, but let's never forget the timeless efficiency of low-tech resilience.

Your MCA approval is not a trademark. 🚫

A founder gets the company name approved, buys the domain, grabs the Instagram handle, prints the packaging.

Then a legal notice arrives.

Why? The MCA register and IP India's Trade Marks Registry are two separate systems under two separate laws. Approval on one carries no legal weight on the other.

What ignoring that gap looks like:

→ Tata Sons: Delhi High Court injunctions against "TATA" look-alikes. A UK-registered "Tata Beauty" lost its domain and social pages and paid ₹5 lakh in costs (2024).

→ Sequoia India: no lawsuit, but a full global rebrand to Peak XV Partners to end brand confusion.

The fix costs ₹0 and one afternoon:
1️⃣ Search IP India's public database (Wordmark + Phonetic + Vienna Code)
2️⃣ Compare every close match on look, sound and meaning
3️⃣ Search every class you're in, plus the ones you'll grow into

Quick vote: what did you check before naming your startup?
A) MCA only
B) Domain / Google
C) IP India trademark search
D) Nothing, just vibes

Drop your letter in the comments. I'll reply to everyone.

posts.title: Frankenstock: The Atkins Tokenization Debacle

Frankenstock: The Atkins Tokenization Debacle

Last Monday, September 14th, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins told a crypto lobby’s summit the quiet part out loud: “Promises were made, and they will be kept.” On Tuesday the 15th, the Senate said no. On Thursday the 17th, he kept his promise anyway.

The result is a sixty-page order called the “Innovation Exemption.” It lets anyone open a stock market by posting a notice on a website. No registration. No rulebook. No Commission vote. No examiner at the door. It lets a stranger tokenize Apple without asking Apple, treating the company’s silence as consent. It puts retail investors, by name, into pools that price by formula, on blockchains where no one has to reverse a theft, and makes the venue post a disclaimer that the SEC never checked any of it. It runs five years, took effect the day it was signed, and opened for comment the same day, which is the SEC’s way of asking your opinion after it has stopped mattering.

Back in May, I made five predictions, and SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce called my warnings “hyperbole.” The order confirms all five in the SEC’s own words.

Any lawyer who reads past the press release will spot it. Every safeguard in this order was lifted from the ninety-two-year-old rulebook Atkins calls obsolete. Nine months ago, when DTCC wanted to tokenize the same stocks, this same agency demanded whitelisted wallets, reversible transfers, and an official record off the chain. On September 17th, it waved all of that away for an industry that raised a $250 million for the last election, wrote an eight-figure check to the inauguration, and watched the SEC drop its cases. In my day we had a word for a regulator whose rulings track the donations. It was not “innovation.”

This is not a story about blockchain. It is a story about capture, featuring an agency built in 1934 to protect investors, now run by a Chairman who took a Solana lobbying stage, promised the room he would deliver with or without Congress, and delivered 48 hours after Congress said no.

I spent almost 20 years inside the SEC and 20 more watching it, and I have never seen anything like the Frankenstock that Atkins has stitched together and jolted to life.

The Stark Reality is that Paul Atkins took an oath to run an agency whose first job is protecting investors. Seventeen months later he headlines crypto lobbying summits, drops the industry’s enforcement cases, and, the moment the Senate refused that industry what it wanted, handed it over himself by decree: five years, no vote, no hearing, no examiner. That is an SEC Chairman gleefully working for the wrong client.

My article documents every step: how the order got issued, what it says, what it concedes, what it contradicts in the SEC’s own DTCC letter, the ten ways it will hurt the people it claims to protect, and why US investors were the only party never consulted. Read it, then ask the question the Senate already answered: who is Paul Atkins actually working for?

Tokenised funds.

It became successful because people could use it seamlessly.

Crypto is following the same path.

Far less noise. More detailed infrastructure.

🏦 37 European banks just agreed to build their euro stablecoin on the same public blockchain people use to trade meme coins.

📌 Qivalis started with 𝟭𝟮 𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗸𝘀 : CaixaBank, BNP Paribas, ING, KBC Bank & Verzekering, UniCredit, DZ BANK AG and BBVA among them and added 𝟮𝟱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 in May, including Spain's Banco Sabadell, Bankinter, Kutxabank, ABANCA and Cecabank. That's 𝟯𝟳 𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝟭𝟱 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 now, Spain alone accounting for 7 of them. The token is euro-backed 1:1, built to run under MiCA's rules, and still needs an e-money license from the Dutch central bank before it can launch, targeted for the second half of this year.

⚡ What actually stood out: they picked 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗘𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘂𝗺, not a private ledger they'd control themselves. Same chain running every DeFi protocol and speculative token a bank's compliance team would normally run from. 37 fairly conservative institutions decided plugging into an existing network of wallets and apps was worth more than keeping full control of the rail.

🧭 Put that next to the European Central Bank's digital euro pilot, running on its own closed infrastructure with 36 hand-picked providers. Same question underneath both (who controls Europe's digital-money rail) and opposite answers. The ECB is building a walled garden. The banks behind Qivalis are betting on the open road.

🔒 That choice isn't free. On a permissionless chain, a bank doesn't fully control the rail its own money runs on… smart-contract risk, network congestion, governance calls all sit with infrastructure the consortium doesn't own. A private ledger avoids all of that. Qivalis is betting reach matters more than control.

💡 Why bother? Whoever settles euro-denominated crypto transactions first owns the layer everyone else builds on top of. Right now that's dollar stablecoins: Tether.io  and Circle  already dominate on-chain volume, euro-denominated included, on the exact network Qivalis is joining.

🔄 Most bank-led blockchain projects I've watched over the years went the opposite direction on purpose: private, permissioned, nothing public-facing, precisely to avoid ceding control. Qivalis reversing that direction, at this scale, is the actual news here. Not that banks are doing stablecoins. That they stopped trying to own the rail outright to get one out fast.

🏧 Neither project has said how you actually cash out. The ECB kept ATM withdrawal out of its pilot scope entirely. Qivalis hasn't said anything yet about redemption through physical infrastructure. Its stated use case stops at "payments and settlement."

🎯 One's a central bank building a closed system. The other is 37 banks betting on open infrastructure they don't control. Worth watching which one figures out how to get the money into someone's hand first, because right now neither has said that's even on the roadmap.

posts.title: Self-custody created a new inheritance problem: ownership can now survive the institution but fail with the individual. The digital keys to vast wealth might be secure on a blockch
posts.author: Wasim Ahmad
posts.snippet:
Self-custody created a new inheritance problem: ownership can now survive the institution but fail with the individual. The digital keys to vast wealth might be secure on a blockchain, but if those keys are lost or inaccessible to heirs, the wealth effectively vanishes. This isn't a niche concern; it's a fundamental challenge arising from digital ownership. We've excelled at granting individuals control, but we've lagged significantly in providing them with robust, understandable mechanisms for passing that control on. What's the most common oversight when people consider their digital estate?

#DigitalInheritance #SelfCustody #CryptoAssets #EstatePlanning
posts.reason: Self-custody inheritance and digital estate planning is a genuine legal problem affecting crypto-holding founders and GCs, opening conversation around testamentary law and key management.

comments.text: There's no EU-wide answer to this yet either - succession law stays national, so a crypto asset held via self-custody by an Estonian domiciled testator with heirs in another member state can raise a private international law question before the technical key-recovery question even arises.
Have you seen estate planning documents actually specify a key-transfer mechanism, or does the digital asset instruction usually stop at 'the executor should locate the wallet'?

We increasingly get asked to build crypto asset provisions into shareholder and founder documentation precisely because standard wills assume a custodian or institution exists to execute against - self-custody removes that assumption entirely.

posts.title: Some fairly sobering reading in the Financial Times this morning.
posts.author: Dr Alexander Culley
posts.snippet:
Some fairly sobering reading in the Financial Times this morning.

According to the article, A7 is a Kremlin-backed network that tries to get around sanctions. It moved at least $6.9 billion through global banks using shell companies, fake invoices, and altered payment details.

It would be easy to just label this as another case of 'Russia, sanctions, and crypto' and move on. However, doing that would miss the bigger issue.

Last month, the National Crime Agency (NCA) warned about A7. While the network does use cryptoassets, the NCA says it relies heavily on regular fiat payments, SWIFT, and correspondent banking too.

The setup is smart, but not particularly unusual.

Russian money is sent to companies in other countries. These companies open local bank accounts and pay international suppliers that look unrelated. They use fake invoices and set up websites, email addresses, and VPNs to make the companies seem local.
This all comes back to screening.

A screening tool can only check the information it receives. If the Russian link is hidden and the payment comes from a company in another country with no obvious connection, there may be no name match at all.

So, it’s important to look closely at the warning signs the NCA lists. These include new companies handling large amounts of business, payments between companies in unrelated industries, invoices that don’t fit the supplier’s usual business, poorly made websites, unclear ownership, and VPN use that doesn’t match the customer’s profile.

If I were an MLRO at a bank, payment institution, or EMI, I’d want to know if our monitoring could connect these dots.

The real question isn’t just whether the sanctions-screening system is running, but whether the whole control setup can spot what’s really happening.

The FT investigation is here:
https://lnkd.in/emWixBxz

The NCA alert is here:
https://lnkd.in/eddMtRqU
#sanctions #financialcrime #payments #aml
posts.reason: Serious discussion of sanctions-evasion, AML monitoring and the role of crypto alongside fiat rails is directly relevant to Lemur Legal's compliance and financial-crime expertise, and invites informed commentary.

comments.text: The point about SWIFT and correspondent banking being the workhorse rather than crypto is worth stressing to anyone doing CASP onboarding due diligence too - too many screening frameworks are still built around the assumption that sanctioned flows will show up as obviously crypto-shaped, when the crypto leg is often the smallest part of the picture.

Given the NCA's emphasis on unrelated-industry payment patterns, are firms actually building that into automated monitoring rules, or is it still mostly caught through manual review by someone who happens to know the sector?

We see the mirror image of this in token issuer due diligence - the ownership obscuring techniques the NCA lists for A7 are strikingly similar to what shows up in some SAFT and TGE structuring when a beneficial owner wants distance from the issuing entity.

posts.title: As accountants, we don't just handle numbers.
posts.author: teamNK
posts.snippet:
As accountants, we don't just handle numbers.

We handle people's lives.

Bank statements.
Payroll details.
Tax returns.
Customer information.
Employee records.
Business strategies.
Passwords and access credentials.

For an accountant working with global clients, data protection and privacy aren't IT issues. They are professional responsibilities.

Here are a few things worth remembering:

1. Access is a privilege, not a right.
Just because you can access a client's information doesn't mean you should.

2. Don't treat confidential data casually.
A spreadsheet emailed to the wrong person can cause more damage than a complicated accounting error.

3. Your client's data travels with your reputation.
One careless incident can undermine years of trust.

4. "It's only accounting data" is a dangerous mindset.
Financial data can reveal salaries, cash flows, customers, investments, weaknesses and future plans.

5. Convenience should never outrank confidentiality.
Personal email, unsecured devices, shared passwords and random file-sharing methods may save a few minutes—but can create enormous risks.

6. Global clients mean global expectations.
Different countries have different privacy laws and contractual requirements. You don't need to be a lawyer—but you do need to understand your responsibility.

7. The weakest link is often human.
Sophisticated systems cannot protect data from someone who forwards the wrong attachment, shares a password or clicks the wrong link.

8. Protect information even after the work is finished.
A completed assignment doesn't mean the client's confidential information becomes yours to keep indefinitely.

9. Train your team.
Data protection is not something you delegate to the IT department. Every accountant handling client information is part of the security chain.

10. Trust is the real currency.
A client may forgive an accounting mistake that gets corrected.
They may find it much harder to forgive a breach of confidentiality.

After all, clients don't outsource their accounting merely because we can prepare their books.

They outsource it because they trust us with what sits behind those books.

And that trust comes with a responsibility:

Handle the numbers professionally.
Handle the data even more carefully.

Passwords and access credentials.

For an accountant working with global clients, data protection and privacy aren't IT issues. They are professional responsibilities.

Here are a few things worth remembering:

1. Access is a privilege, not a right.
Just because you can access a client's information doesn't mean you should.

2. Don't treat confidential data casually.
A spreadsheet emailed to the wrong person can cause more damage than a complicated accounting error.

3. Your client's data travels with your reputation.
One careless incident can undermine years of trust.

4. "It's only accounting data" is a dangerous mindset.
Financial data can reveal salaries, cash flows, customers, investments, weaknesses and future plans.

5. Convenience should never outrank confidentiality.
Personal email, unsecured devices, shared passwords and random file-sharing methods may save a few minutes—but can create enormous risks.

6. Global clients mean global expectations.
Different countries have different privacy laws and contractual requirements. You don't need to be a lawyer—but you do need to understand your responsibility.

7. The weakest link is often human.
Sophisticated systems cannot protect data from someone who forwards the wrong attachment, shares a password or clicks the wrong link.

8. Protect information even after the work is finished.
A completed assignment doesn't mean the client's confidential information becomes yours to keep indefinitely.

9. Train your team.
Data protection is not something you delegate to the IT department. Every accountant handling client information is part of the security chain.

10. Trust is the real currency.
A client may forgive an accounting mistake that gets corrected.
They may find it much harder to forgive a breach of confidentiality.

After all, clients don't outsource their accounting merely because we can prepare their books.

They outsource it because they trust us with what sits behind those books.

And that trust comes with a responsibility:

Handle the numbers professionally.
Handle the data even more carefully.

posts.title: What can Marketing learn from Learning - and vice versa?
posts.author: Vincent Ganne
posts.snippet:
What can Marketing learn from Learning - and vice versa?

A headhunter asked me last week how similar Marketing and Learning really are, having seen me straddle both for 20 years. My short answer: both are about winning people over and changing what they do.

The longer answer: each is strongest where the other is weakest. Marketing is obsessive about attention, audience and conversion. Learning is obsessive about practice, progress and whether the change lasts.

Here are 3 practices from each that I keep coming back to.

𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴

1. Earn their attention - don't assume it
Marketers know that if the subject line doesn't land, nothing else gets read. Learning often assumes a captive audience. If anything, that makes the first five minutes matter even more: what's in it for them?

2. Run it as a campaign, not an event
A good campaign is never one email. It's a sequence: teaser, launch, follow-ups, and a nudge for whoever went quiet. Most training lasts a day and then... silence. What happens before (why should I care?) and after (what do I do differently on Monday?) is where the learning is won or lost.

3. Design for word of mouth
Marketing plans for referral from day one. Learning rarely plans for the learner who teaches a colleague. Yet nothing clarifies your understanding like having to explain it to someone else. That's what makes it stick - and how it spreads across an organisation.

𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

1. Make them do something
We remember what we work out far better than what we're told. When I built the Practitioner's Blueprint diagnostic, the point was for people to reflect on their own gaps. More often than not, an assessment or a trial beats a static whitepaper.

2. Space it and mix it up
A baseball study had one group practise the same pitch 15 times in a row, while the other faced a mix of pitches. The mixed group struggled more in training but hit far better afterwards. Rather than the same message 15 times, there's a real case for interweaving your strategic themes, returning to each from a different angle.

3. Measure the change, not the click
Happy sheets tell you people enjoyed the programme. NPS tells you they'd recommend you. Neither tells you whether anything changed. At Firefly, the number I trusted most was revenue retention: were schools still with us a year on?

Where marketing and learning meet most closely is post-sale. The best engagement campaigns feel like a great learning experience: peers to learn from, progress worth celebrating, reassurance you're on the right track. Get that right, and customers stay and bring in the next ones - a Virtuous Cycle. As AI makes acquisition noisier, I'd expect that's where the battleground will move.

Which of the six would you add to, or cut?

posts.title: AI is transforming software development, but it shouldn't bypass corporate governance.
posts.author: Brij Bhan Singh

AI is transforming software development, but it shouldn't bypass corporate governance. 

Yesterday, I had an insightful discussion with my colleagues at Xoriant about the evolution of our Corporate Audit portfolio and its critical relevance in the age of AI. 
The consensus? AI accelerates velocity, but speed without guardrails is a liability. If AI tools are not implemented securely—without strict compliance, RBAC, least privilege access, and segregation of duties—things will go wrong. 
A modern Corporate Audit portfolio must act as a centralized, organized system of record for Audit Activities, Compliance, Risk Assessment, and Testing. 

To build responsibly, we break it down into Who, What, and How:
🔹 Governance (Who): Who is in charge and who establishes the rules?
🔹 Risk Management (What): What can go wrong, and how do we proactively stop it?
🔹 Compliance (How): Are internal rules, industry standards, and regulatory compliance being strictly followed? 

When developing AI-driven or enterprise applications, these 4 pillars are non-negotiable:
1.  Immutable Audit Trails: Every action must be permanently logged and tamper-proof.
2.  RBAC: Strict Role-Based Access Controls to enforce least privilege access.
3.  Segregation of Duties (SOD): Clear boundaries (e.g., a developer's Pull Request must always be reviewed by another team member).
4.  Data Retention: Clear pipelines to archive or delete data in strict alignment with government laws and corporate policies. 
5. Jira & Project Governance: Each user story must feature well-defined Acceptance Criteria (AC) and clear dependencies. Essential tasks—including development, peer reviews, PR and testing—must be explicitly tracked, with test results automatically attached directly to the Jira task through automated pipelines.

Ensure quality and security through the 3 Lines of Defence:
Line 1: Tech & Operations – Building inherently secure, resilient systems from day one.
Line 2: Risk & Compliance – Ensuring 100% adherence to regulatory compliance rules.
Line 3: Corporate Audit Team – Conducting periodic, independent reviews of project documentation, code quality, and testing artifacts. 

Innovation thrives when it’s built on a foundation of trust. How is your organization adapting its audit and compliance frameworks for the AI era? 

I am interested to hear how other industry leaders are structuring their lines of defense for AI-driven applications.

posts.author: Kingsley Egbuonu
posts.snippet:
Another day, another decision against a big US tech company. This time Meta could not rely on the hosting defence before the Frankfurt Regional Court, Germany, because of its algorithmic and ad auction systems.

Finflow GmbH (owner of Finanzfluss) and one of its founders, Thomas Kehl, sued Meta for allowing the unauthorised use of their photos and registered trade marks in fake investment posts on Instagram and Facebook. They largely succeeded.

I understand the outcomes were as follows:
1️⃣ The company's copyright claim didn't succeed on ownership grounds.

2️⃣ The company's trade mark infringement claim succeeded.

3️⃣ Kehl's personality/image right and the company's "corporate personality" claims succeeded.

4️⃣ Meta's reliance on the "safe harbour" or "hosting" defence under the Digital Services Act failed because of the algorithmic and ad auction systems powering its platforms, its knowledge of the infringing acts, and its failure to stop them promptly and effectively.

5️⃣ Among other things, Meta was ordered to prevent the publication of such posts; provide an account of the scale of the infringements and revenues generated from them; and pay compensation and legal costs.

Meta can still appeal. See Oliver Löffel's commentary on this decision, including the impact of the CJEU's WebGroup/Coyote decision, and Marco Bassini's comments on the CJEU's decision in AGCOM v Google.

posts.title: I am happy to share my new publication: "Regulating Life Technologies at the Nanoscale: EU-US Comparative Perspectives on Dynamic Licensing under Deep Uncertainty", published in th
posts.author: Umberto Nizza
posts.snippet:
I am happy to share my new publication: "Regulating Life Technologies at the Nanoscale: EU-US Comparative Perspectives on Dynamic Licensing under Deep Uncertainty", published in the Transatlantic Technology Law Forum Working Paper Series at Stanford Law School. 
📖 The paper is available here:
https://lnkd.in/eQ8zhNAa

In this paper, I argue that nanotechnology reveals a peculiar regulatory problem, shared by many emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and synthetic biology: legal authorization is often granted before the relevant risks can be scientifically understood. Traditional regulatory models, however, assume precisely the opposite, supposing that uncertainty can be translated into measurable probabilities before legal decisions are taken. 
Building on a comparative analysis of the European precautionary approach and the American post-market model, I show that both frameworks are efficient only under conditions that nanotechnology systematically violates. In this perspective, the paper develops a formal law and economics model of dynamic licensing, in which regulatory authorization, monitoring obligations, and compliance requirements evolve continuously as scientific knowledge develops. Rather than treating authorization as a binary decision, regulation becomes an adaptive learning process capable of responding to deep uncertainty.
Beyond nanotechnology, the proposed framework offers a general model for regulating technologies whose risk profiles evolve throughout commercialization, suggesting that the most efficient legal system is neither the most precautionary nor the most permissive, but the one that institutionalizes learning.

⚖️ The Takeaway
When science cannot provide definitive answers at the moment regulation begins, the solution is not to choose between ex ante precaution and ex post correction. The challenge is to design legal institutions capable of cutting-edge learning as scientific knowledge evolves.

posts.title: The EU AI Act's high-risk classification rules are starting to bite for financial services, and it's worth understanding exactly what falls into that category before it becomes a c
posts.author: Be1B - Embedded Finance SaaS
posts.snippet:
The EU AI Act's high-risk classification rules are starting to bite for financial services, and it's worth understanding exactly what falls into that category before it becomes a compliance scramble.

Credit scoring and creditworthiness assessment are explicitly classified as high-risk under the Act, which means any AI system used to make or meaningfully influence a lending decision now carries specific obligations: documented risk management, human oversight requirements, and transparency obligations toward the people affected by the decision.

What's often missed: back-office AI, fraud detection, reconciliation, KYB document processing, generally falls outside the high-risk category, because it doesn't directly determine an individual's access to a financial product or service.

That distinction matters enormously for where AI investment gets deployed first. Front-office, customer-affecting AI now carries real regulatory weight before deployment. Back-office AI largely doesn't, which is a big part of why we keep seeing faster, cleaner adoption there.

If your organisation is planning AI deployment across both categories, worth mapping which systems actually fall under high-risk obligations before building, not after.

Has this classification changed how your team is sequencing AI investment?
